blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 2 (Force and Motion), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question of 5 marks (define, explain, derive) is followed by a numerical of 3 marks on the same topic. Each question has a model answer; the numericals are solved step by step.

blocks.prompt: 1 What are rectangular components of a vector? Find the rectangular components of a vector A making an angle θ with the x-axis, and show how the magnitude and direction of A are found from its components. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Component: the effective value of a vector in a given direction. Components along mutually perpendicular directions are called rectangular components.

Resolution: Let vector A be represented by line OP making angle θ with the x-axis (Fig. 2.1). Draw projection OM on the x-axis and ON on the y-axis. OM represents Ax and ON (= MP) represents Ay. By the head to tail rule:
A = Ax + Ay ... (2.1)
In the right-angled triangle OMP:
Ax = A cos θ ... (2.2)
Ay = A sin θ ... (2.3)

Magnitude from components: In right-angled triangle OMP, by the Pythagorean theorem,
(OP)² = (OM)² + (MP)², or A² = Ax² + Ay² ... (2.4)
A = √(Ax² + Ay²)

Direction: tan θ = MP/OM = Ay/Ax, so θ = tan⁻¹(Ay/Ax) ... (2.5)

blocks.prompt: 2 A force of 6 N acts along the x-axis and a force of 8 N acts at 60° to the x-axis on the same body. Find the magnitude and direction of their resultant. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Add the x-components and the y-components separately, then use Pythagoras and tan⁻¹.

book_ref.quote: Let θ be the angle between two forces F₁ and F₂, where F₁ is along x-axis.

steps: Rx = F₁ cos 0° + F₂ cos 60° = 6 + 8 × 0.5 = 10 N
blocks.final_answer: Resultant = 12.2 N at 34.7° to the x-axis

blocks.prompt: 3 Define the scalar product of two vectors and give its physical interpretation. Show that work is a scalar product. Also write the scalar product in terms of rectangular components and use it to find the angle between two vectors. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: The scalar product of A and B is A.B = AB cos θ ... (2.6), where A and B are the magnitudes and θ is the angle between them. The result is a scalar.

Physical interpretation: Bring A and B to a common origin (Fig. 2.2).
A.B = A (projection of B on A) = A (B cos θ) = AB cos θ
Similarly B.A = B (A cos θ) = BA cos θ

Work as a scalar product: A force F moves its point of application a distance d at angle θ to its line of action (Fig. 2.3).
Work done = (effective component of force in the direction of motion) × distance moved = (F cos θ)d = Fd cos θ
In vector notation: F.d = Fd cos θ = work done

In terms of rectangular components:
A.B = AxBx + AyBy + AzBz ... (2.7)
Since A.B = AB cos θ, the angle between two vectors is
cos θ = (AxBx + AyBy + AzBz)/AB ... (2.8)

Characteristics: A.B = B.A (commutative); A.B = 0 for perpendicular vectors; A.B = AB for parallel and -AB for antiparallel vectors; A.A = A².

book_ref.quote: The scalar product of two vectors A⃗ and B⃗ is written as A⃗.B⃗ and is defined as

blocks.prompt: 4 Vector A has components Ax = 2, Ay = 3, Az = 6 and vector B has components Bx = 3, By = 4, Bz = 0. Find A.B and the angle between A and B. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find A.B from components, the two magnitudes from Pythagoras, then cos θ = A.B/AB.

book_ref.quote: Equation (2.6) can be used to find the angle between two vectors. Since,

blocks.prompt: 5 Define the vector product of two vectors. How is its direction found? Describe its characteristics and give two examples from physics. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: The vector product of A and B is a vector:
A × B = AB sin θ n̂ ... (2.9)
where n̂ is a unit vector perpendicular to the plane containing A and B.

Direction (right hand rule): Place the tails of A and B together to define their plane. The product vector is perpendicular to this plane. Rotate the first vector A into B through the smaller angle, curling the fingers of the right hand in the direction of rotation with the thumb erect; the thumb gives the direction of A × B (Fig. 2.4 b).

Characteristics:
1. Non-commutative: A × B ≠ B × A; in fact A × B = -B × A ... (2.10)
2. For perpendicular vectors (θ = 90°) the magnitude is maximum: A × B = AB n̂
3. For parallel vectors (θ = 0° or 180°) it is a null vector; hence A × A = 0
4. |A × B| equals the area of the parallelogram with A and B as adjacent sides (Fig. 2.4 d)

Examples:
(i) Torque: τ = r × F, the turning effect of force F applied at position vector r.
(ii) Force on charge q moving with velocity v in magnetic field B: F = q(v × B).

book_ref.quote: place together the tail of vectors A⃗ and B⃗ to define the plane of vectors A⃗ and B⃗

blocks.prompt: 6 Two vectors of magnitudes 6 units and 4 units make an angle of 30° with each other. Find (i) the magnitude of their vector product (ii) their scalar product (iii) the area of the parallelogram having these vectors as adjacent sides. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use AB sin θ for the cross product (which is also the area) and AB cos θ for the dot product.

book_ref.quote: The magnitude of A⃗ x B⃗ is equal to the area of the parallelogram

steps: |A × B| = AB sin θ = 6 × 4 × sin 30° = 24 × 0.5 = 12 units
A.B = AB cos θ = 6 × 4 × cos 30° = 24 × 0.866 = 20.8 units
Area of parallelogram = |A × B| = 12 square units
blocks.final_answer: |A × B| = 12 units; A.B = 20.8 units; area = 12 square units

blocks.prompt: 7 State the condition under which the equations of motion apply. Derive the first equation of motion (i) from the definition of acceleration (ii) from the velocity-time graph. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Condition: The equations of motion apply only to objects moving in a straight line with constant acceleration. The first equation relates velocity and time.

(i) From the definition of acceleration: A body moving with uniform acceleration a changes its velocity from vi to vf in time t. Then
a = (vf - vi)/t
vf - vi = at
vf = vi + at ... (2.11)

(ii) Graphical method: In the velocity-time graph (Fig. 2.5) the velocity is vi at A and vf at B after time t. Draw BD perpendicular to the x-axis and BE perpendicular to the y-axis.
OA = vi (initial velocity), BD = vf (final velocity)
BD = BC + CD = BC + OA (as OA = CD)
vf = BC + vi ... (2.12)
The slope of line AB is the acceleration: a = BC/AC, and AC = t, so a = BC/t, or BC = at ... (2.13)
Combining (2.12) and (2.13): vf = at + vi, or vf = vi + at.
This is the first equation of motion.

book_ref.quote: A perpendicular BD is drawn from point B to x-axis

blocks.prompt: 8 A bus moving at 4 m s⁻¹ accelerates uniformly at 1.5 m s⁻² for 8 s. Find its final velocity. How long would it take to reach 25 m s⁻¹ from the start? (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use vf = vi + at for the velocity, then rearrange it as t = (vf - vi)/a for the time.

book_ref.quote: Above equation is the first equation of motion.

steps: Given: vi = 4 m s⁻¹, a = 1.5 m s⁻², t = 8 s
blocks.final_answer: vf = 16 m s⁻¹ after 8 s; 25 m s⁻¹ is reached after 14 s

blocks.prompt: 9 Derive the second equation of motion S = vit + ½at² (i) by using average velocity (ii) by the graphical method. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Using average velocity: A body with uniform acceleration a has initial velocity vi, final velocity vf after time t, and covers displacement S. Since the velocity is not constant, we use average velocity:
Displacement = average velocity × time
S = (vi + vf)/2 × t
Using the first equation vf = vi + at:
S = (vi + vi + at)/2 × t = (2vi + at)/2 × t
2S = 2vit + at²
S = vit + ½at² ... (2.14)

(ii) Graphical method: In the velocity-time graph (Fig. 2.6) the displacement equals the area under the graph:
S = area of figure OABD = area of rectangle OACD + area of triangle ABC
S = (OA × OD) + ½(AC × BC)
With OA = vi and OD = AC = t: S = vi × t + ½(t × BC)
From the first equation (graph), BC = at:
S = vit + ½(t × at) = vit + ½at²
This is the second equation of motion.

book_ref.quote: While moving with constant acceleration a it covers a displacement S in time t.

blocks.prompt: 10 A cyclist moving at 3 m s⁻¹ accelerates uniformly at 0.4 m s⁻² for 10 s. Find the distance covered in this time and the final velocity. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use S = vit + ½at² for distance and vf = vi + at for velocity; check with S = (vi + vf)/2 × t.

book_ref.quote: This is the second equation of motion.

steps: Given: vi = 3 m s⁻¹, a = 0.4 m s⁻², t = 10 s

blocks.prompt: 11 Derive the third equation of motion 2aS = vf² - vi² (i) from the average velocity (ii) by the graphical method. How are these equations applied to freely falling bodies? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) From the average velocity: A body moving in a straight line has initial velocity vi, final velocity vf after time t, and displacement S.
S = (vi + vf)/2 × t, so 2S = (vi + vf) × t ... (2.15)
From the first equation vf = vi + at, t = (vf - vi)/a. Putting t in (2.15):
2S = (vf + vi)(vf - vi)/a
2aS = vf² - vi²

(ii) Graphical method: In the velocity-time graph (Fig. 2.7) the distance S is the area OABD under the graph, a trapezium:
S = ½ (sum of parallel sides) × height = ½ (OA + BD) × OD
Since OA = vi, BD = vf and OD = t: S = ½(vi + vf) × t
From the first equation t = (vf - vi)/a, so
S = ½(vf + vi)(vf - vi)/a
2aS = vf² - vi² ... (2.16)

Free fall: In the absence of air resistance, bodies fall with uniform acceleration g (average value 9.8 m s⁻², downward). Putting a = g:
vf = vi + gt; h = vit + ½gt²; vf² - vi² = 2gh
g is taken positive for a falling body (vi = 0) and negative for a body projected vertically upward.

book_ref.quote: In the speed time graph shown in the figure

blocks.prompt: 12 A car moving at 90 km h⁻¹ is brought to rest with uniform retardation in a distance of 125 m. Find (i) its acceleration (ii) the time taken to stop. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Convert km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹, use 2aS = vf² - vi² (time is not given), then vf = vi + at for the time.

book_ref.quote: This is the third equation of motion.

blocks.prompt: 13 What is projectile motion? Explain the motion of a projectile fired at angle θ with the horizontal by resolving it into horizontal and vertical components, and find the magnitude and direction of its velocity at any instant. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Projectile motion is two dimensional motion under constant acceleration due to gravity. Examples: a football kicked by a player, a ball thrown by a cricketer, a missile fired from a launching pad.

Thrown horizontally: For a ball thrown horizontally with velocity vx from a height, no horizontal force acts (air friction ignored), so x = vx × t ... (2.17). The vertical motion is free fall from zero vertical velocity: y = ½gt².

Fired at angle θ (Fig. 2.8 b): Resolve vi into vi cos θ (horizontal) and vi sin θ (vertical). The two motions are independent.
Horizontal: ax = 0 (air resistance neglected, no horizontal force), so the horizontal component stays constant:
vfx = vix = vi cos θ ... (2.18)
Vertical: ay = -g for the upward motion; by the first equation of motion:
vfy = vi sin θ - gt ... (2.19)

Velocity at any instant:
Magnitude: v = √(vfx² + vfy²) ... (2.20)
Direction with the horizontal: tan φ = vfy/vfx ... (2.21)

book_ref.quote: the motion of a projectile can be studied easily by resolving it into horizontal and vertical components

blocks.prompt: 14 A ball is thrown horizontally at 12 m s⁻¹ from the top of a building 44.1 m high. Find (i) the time to reach the ground (ii) the horizontal distance covered (iii) its velocity on striking the ground. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: The vertical motion is free fall from zero vertical velocity; the horizontal velocity stays 12 m s⁻¹. Combine the two components at the end.

book_ref.quote: Suppose that the ball leaves the hand of the thrower at point A

steps: Vertical: y = ½gt², so t = √(2y/g) = √(2 × 44.1/9.8) = √9 = 3 s
vfy = gt = 9.8 × 3 = 29.4 m s⁻¹ (downward); vfx = 12 m s⁻¹
v = √(12² + 29.4²) = 31.8 m s⁻¹; tan φ = 29.4/12, φ = 67.8° below the horizontal
blocks.final_answer: t = 3 s; x = 36 m; v = 31.8 m s⁻¹ at 67.8° below the horizontal

blocks.prompt: 15 Define the time of flight and the maximum height of a projectile. Derive their expressions for a projectile fired from the ground with velocity vi at angle θ. What is the effect of air resistance on the height? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Time of flight: the time taken by the body from the place of projection to the place where it hits the ground.
The body goes up and comes back to the same level, so its vertical displacement S = h = 0. The vertical component of velocity is vi sin θ and a = -g:
S = vit + ½at² gives 0 = vi sin θ t - ½gt²
Dividing by t: t = 2vi sin θ / g ... (2.23)

Maximum height: Using 2aS = vf² - vi² for the vertical motion, with a = -g, initial vertical velocity vi sin θ, and vertical velocity 0 at the highest point, S = h:
-2gh = 0 - vi² sin²θ
h = vi² sin²θ / 2g ... (2.22)

Air resistance: it decreases the upward velocity of the projectile, so the height reached is reduced.

book_ref.quote: Hence, the equation of motion is:

blocks.prompt: 16 A shell is fired from the ground at 40 m s⁻¹ at 60° above the horizontal. Find (i) its time of flight (ii) the maximum height it reaches. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Only the vertical component vi sin θ decides both answers; use the two formulas derived above.

book_ref.quote: the initial vertical velocity viy = vi sin θ

blocks.final_answer: Time of flight = 7.07 s; maximum height = 61.2 m

blocks.prompt: 17 Define the range of a projectile and derive its expression. On what does it depend? How do the height and range change for angles below and above 45°, and how does air resistance affect the range and the path? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Range: the maximum distance which a projectile covers in the horizontal direction.

Derivation: Multiply the horizontal component of the velocity of projection by the total time of flight:
R = vix × t = vi cos θ × (2vi sin θ / g)
R = (vi²/g) 2 sin θ cos θ
As 2 sin θ cos θ = sin 2θ:
R = (vi²/g) sin 2θ ... (2.24)
So the range depends on the velocity of projection and the angle of projection.

Maximum range: R is maximum when sin 2θ = 1, i.e. 2θ = 90°, θ = 45°.
For an angle less than 45°, both the height and the range are less; for an angle larger than 45°, the height is more but the range is again less.

Air resistance: it slows the forward motion and reduces vi, so the range decreases. It is not constant during the flight (it decreases as the object slows down), so the path is not a perfect parabola but skewed, with a steeper descent than ascent; a high-speed projectile falls short of the parabolic path.

book_ref.quote: As 2 sin θ cos θ = sin 2θ

blocks.prompt: 18 A ball is kicked from level ground at 35 m s⁻¹. Find its range when it is kicked at (i) 45° (ii) 30° to the horizontal. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Apply R = (vi²/g) sin 2θ for each angle; 45° should give the larger range.

book_ref.quote: Determine the height to which it rises, the time of flight and the horizontal range.

blocks.final_answer: R = 125 m at 45°; R = 108 m at 30° (the range is maximum at 45°)

blocks.prompt: 19 Define linear momentum and impulse. Show that the change in momentum of a body equals the product of force and time, and hence state Newton's second law in terms of momentum. Why is this form more general than F = ma? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Linear momentum: p = mv ... (2.25). It is a vector in the direction of velocity; SI unit kg m s⁻¹ (= N s).

Relation with force: A body of mass m has initial velocity vi. An external force F acts on it for time t, after which its velocity is vf. The acceleration is
a = (vf - vi)/t
By Newton's second law, a = F/m. Equating:
F/m = (vf - vi)/t
F × t = mvf - mvi ... (2.26)
where mvi is the initial and mvf the final momentum. So the change in momentum equals the product of force and the time for which it acts.

Second law in terms of momentum: F = (mvf - mvi)/t, i.e. the time rate of change of momentum of a body is equal to the applied force.

Impulse: when a force acts for a very short time and varies from instant to instant (e.g. a bat hitting a ball), we use the product of the average force and the time:
Impulse = F × t = mvf - mvi ... (2.27)

More general: this form can be extended to cases where the mass changes while the body accelerates, e.g. a rocket that loses mass as its fuel is burnt and ejected.

book_ref.quote: Suppose an external force F⃗ acts upon it for time t after which velocity becomes

blocks.prompt: 20 A 0.15 kg ball reaches a batsman at 30 m s⁻¹ and is hit straight back at 20 m s⁻¹. The bat is in contact with the ball for 0.01 s. Find (i) the impulse on the ball (ii) the average force exerted by the bat. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Momentum is a vector: give the returning velocity the opposite sign, then impulse = mvf - mvi and F = impulse/t.

book_ref.quote: How large was the average retarding force?

steps: Take the incoming direction positive: vi = +30 m s⁻¹, vf = -20 m s⁻¹
blocks.final_answer: Impulse = 7.5 N s and average force = 750 N, both directed back towards the bowler (opposite to the incoming ball)

blocks.prompt: 21 What is an isolated system? Derive the law of conservation of linear momentum for two colliding balls and state the law. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Isolated system: a system on which no external agency exerts any force, e.g. molecules of a gas enclosed in a glass vessel at constant temperature.

Derivation: Two smooth hard balls of masses m1 and m2 move along the same straight line in the same direction with velocities v1 and v2. They collide; afterwards their velocities are v1′ and v2′ (Fig. 2.9). During the collision (time t), ball 2 exerts force F on ball 1 and ball 1 exerts F′ on ball 2. Using F × t = change in momentum:
For m1: F × t = m1v1′ - m1v1
For m2: F′ × t = m2v2′ - m2v2
Adding: (F + F′) t = (m1v1′ - m1v1) + (m2v2′ - m2v2)
Action and reaction are equal and opposite: F′ = -F, so F + F′ = 0:
0 = (m1v1′ - m1v1) + (m2v2′ - m2v2)
m1v1 + m2v2 = m1v1′ + m2v2′ ... (2.28)
Total momentum before collision = total momentum after collision; the total change in momentum of the isolated system is zero.

Law: The total linear momentum of an isolated system remains constant.
Since momentum is a vector, directions (signs) must be taken into account when applying it.

book_ref.quote: Adding these two expressions, we have

blocks.prompt: 22 A 4 kg ball moving at 5 m s⁻¹ and a 6 kg ball moving at 2 m s⁻¹ approach each other and collide. After the collision the 4 kg ball moves back at 1 m s⁻¹. Find the velocity of the 6 kg ball after the collision. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Choose the 4 kg ball's initial direction as positive, give opposite velocities a negative sign, and equate total momentum before and after.

book_ref.quote: What must be the velocity of the smaller ball after collision

steps: Conservation: 8 = -4 + 6 v2′, so v2′ = 12/6 = 2 m s⁻¹
blocks.final_answer: v2′ = +2 m s⁻¹: the 6 kg ball moves at 2 m s⁻¹ in the original direction of the 4 kg ball (it is turned back)

blocks.prompt: 23 Distinguish elastic from inelastic collisions. For an elastic collision of two balls in one dimension, show that the relative velocity of approach equals the relative velocity of separation, write the final velocities, and discuss the cases m1 = m2 with v2 = 0, and a light body hitting a massive body at rest. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Elastic collision: no K.E. is lost (perfectly elastic). Inelastic collision: K.E. of the system is not conserved. Momentum and total energy are conserved in all collisions.

Two smooth, non-rotating balls m1, m2 move in the same direction with v1, v2 and after collision with v1′, v2′ (Fig. 2.10). Positive direction to the right.
Momentum: m1v1 + m2v2 = m1v1′ + m2v2′
m1(v1 - v1′) = m2(v2′ - v2) ... (2.29)
K.E. (elastic): ½m1v1² + ½m2v2² = ½m1v1′² + ½m2v2′²
m1(v1² - v1′²) = m2(v2′² - v2²)
m1(v1 + v1′)(v1 - v1′) = m2(v2′ + v2)(v2′ - v2) ... (2.30)
Dividing (2.30) by (2.29):
v1 + v1′ = v2′ + v2 ... (2.31)
(v1 - v2) = (v2′ - v1′) = -(v1′ - v2′)
So the relative velocity has the same magnitude before and after but is reversed: relative velocity of approach = relative velocity of separation (in magnitude).

Solving (2.29) and (2.30):
v1′ = (m1 - m2)/(m1 + m2) v1 + 2m2/(m1 + m2) v2 ... (2.32)
v2′ = 2m1/(m1 + m2) v1 + (m2 - m1)/(m1 + m2) v2 ... (2.33)

Case m1 = m2, v2 = 0: v1′ = 0, v2′ = v1. The first ball stops and the second moves off with its velocity (billiard balls).
Case m2 >> m1, v2 = 0: v1′ = -v1, v2′ = 0. The light ball bounces back with the same speed (used by the squash player).

book_ref.quote: By applying the law of conservation of momentum we have

blocks.prompt: 24 A 0.2 kg ball moving at 5 m s⁻¹ makes a head-on elastic collision with a 0.3 kg ball at rest. Find the velocities of both balls after the collision and show that kinetic energy is conserved. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Put v2 = 0 in Eqs. (2.32) and (2.33), then compare the total K.E. before and after.

book_ref.quote: If the collision were perfectly elastic.

blocks.final_answer: v1′ = -1 m s⁻¹ (rebounds), v2′ = 4 m s⁻¹; K.E. = 2.5 J before and after, so it is conserved

blocks.prompt: 25 What is meant by an elastic collision in two dimensions? For a projectile m1 striking a target m2 at rest, write the conservation equations along the x- and y-axes and for kinetic energy, and explain how they show that a collision is elastic. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Two-dimensional collision: bodies travelling along an axis do not end up travelling along the same axis after the collision (a glancing, not head-on collision). When it is elastic, both total linear momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved.

Setup (Fig. 2.15): projectile m1 moves along the x-axis with v1i; target m2 is at rest (v2i = 0). After collision they move with v1f at θ1 and v2f at θ2 to the x-axis, on opposite sides.
Initial momentum = m1v1i (along x); the target's is zero. Resolve m1v1f into m1v1f cos θ1 and m1v1f sin θ1, and m2v2f into m2v2f cos θ2 and m2v2f sin θ2.

x-axis: m1v1i = m1v1f cos θ1 + m2v2f cos θ2
m1v1i - m1v1f cos θ1 = m2v2f cos θ2 ... (2.34)
y-axis: 0 = m1v1f sin θ1 - m2v2f sin θ2
m1v1f sin θ1 = m2v2f sin θ2 ... (2.35)
Kinetic energy: ½m1v1i² = ½m1v1f² + ½m2v2f²
m1v1i² = m1v1f² + m2v2f² ... (2.36)

There are four unknowns, v1f, v2f, θ1 and θ2. If they are measured and satisfy (2.34), (2.35) and (2.36), momentum and K.E. are both conserved and the collision is elastic.

book_ref.quote: The initial momentum of projectile before collision is m₁v⃗₁i

blocks.prompt: 26 A 2 kg ball moving at 5 m s⁻¹ along the x-axis strikes an identical ball at rest. After the collision the first ball moves at 4 m s⁻¹ at 37° above the x-axis and the second at 3 m s⁻¹ at 53° below it. Show that momentum is conserved along both axes and that the collision is elastic. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Check Eq. (2.34) along x, Eq. (2.35) along y, and Eq. (2.36) for K.E.

book_ref.quote: is moving with initial velocity 5 m s⁻¹ towards right collides with stationary target

steps: x: before m1v1i = 2 × 5 = 10 kg m s⁻¹; after 2 × 4 cos 37° + 2 × 3 cos 53° = 6.39 + 3.61 = 10.0 kg m s⁻¹
y: before 0; after 2 × 4 sin 37° - 2 × 3 sin 53° = 4.81 - 4.79 = 0.02 ≈ 0 (the tiny difference comes only from rounding the angles to 37° and 53°)
K.E. before = ½ × 2 × 5² = 25 J; after = ½ × 2 × 4² + ½ × 2 × 3² = 16 + 9 = 25 J
blocks.final_answer: Momentum is conserved along x and y, and K.E. = 25 J before and after: the collision is elastic

blocks.prompt: 27 What is a perfectly inelastic collision? For such a collision in one dimension, find the common velocity of the bodies and show that the fraction of kinetic energy lost is m2/(m1 + m2) when the target is at rest. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
A perfectly inelastic collision is one in which the colliding bodies stick together and move as a single body after the collision. Momentum is conserved but K.E. is not.

Common velocity: Bodies m1 (projectile) and m2 (target) move along the same line with v1i and v2i (v1i > v2i), collide and stick; the combined mass m1 + m2 moves with vf (Fig. 2.16). By conservation of momentum:
m1v1i + m2v2i = (m1 + m2)vf
vf = m1/(m1 + m2) v1i + m2/(m1 + m2) v2i
If the target is at rest (v2i = 0):
vf = m1/(m1 + m2) v1i ... (2.37)
The velocity of m1 is reduced by the mass ratio m1/(m1 + m2); the larger m1, the faster the combination moves.

Kinetic energy:
(K.E)i = ½m1v1i² + ½m2v2i²; (K.E)f = ½(m1 + m2)vf²
Fraction lost = [(K.E)i - (K.E)f]/(K.E)i
With v2i = 0 and vf from (2.37):
= [½m1v1i² - ½(m1 + m2)(m1/(m1 + m2))² v1i²]/(½m1v1i²)
= 1 - m1/(m1 + m2)
= m2/(m1 + m2) ... (2.38)
So kinetic energy is lost in an inelastic collision in one dimension.

book_ref.quote: Since the collision is perfectly inelastic, the total momentum of balls is conserved.

blocks.prompt: 28 A 3 kg trolley moving at 8 m s⁻¹ collides with a 1 kg trolley at rest and they move off together. Find (i) the common velocity (ii) the K.E. lost (iii) check the fraction lost with m2/(m1 + m2). (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use Eq. (2.37) for vf, compute both kinetic energies, then compare the lost fraction with Eq. (2.38).

book_ref.quote: Show law of conservation of momentum and energy losses during perfect inelastic collision.

blocks.final_answer: vf = 6 m s⁻¹; K.E. lost = 24 J (one quarter of the initial K.E.)

blocks.prompt: 29 Explain a perfectly inelastic collision in two dimensions. Write the momentum equations along the x- and y-axes and obtain the magnitude and direction of the common final velocity. How is the loss of kinetic energy found? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Macroscopic collisions are generally inelastic and do not conserve K.E. In a perfectly inelastic collision the bodies stick together to make a single mass.

Two bodies m1 and m2 move in the xy-plane with velocities v1i and v2i at angles θ1 and θ2 to the x-axis and collide at the origin (Fig. 2.17). After collision the combined mass M = m1 + m2 moves with vf at angle φ to the x-axis. Resolving velocities into components:
x-direction: m1v1i cos θ1 + m2v2i cos θ2 = Mvf cos φ ... (2.39)
y-direction: m1v1i sin θ1 + m2v2i sin θ2 = Mvf sin φ ... (2.40)

Magnitude (square and add (2.39) and (2.40)):
vf = √{[(m1v1i cos θ1 + m2v2i cos θ2)/M]² + [(m1v1i sin θ1 + m2v2i sin θ2)/M]²} ... (2.41)
Direction (divide (2.40) by (2.39)):
φ = tan⁻¹[(m1v1i sin θ1 + m2v2i sin θ2)/(m1v1i cos θ1 + m2v2i cos θ2)] ... (2.42)

Kinetic energy (a scalar, so no components needed):
(K.E)i = ½m1v1i² + ½m2v2i² ... (2.43)
(K.E)f = ½Mvf² ... (2.44)
Loss: Δ(K.E) = (K.E)i - (K.E)f; this energy is transformed into heat, sound or deformation.

blocks.prompt: 31 Explain the principle of rocket propulsion. Why can a rocket work where there is no air, why are rockets built in several linked parts, and how does its acceleration change during the flight? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Principle: Rockets move by expelling burning gas through engines at their rear. Fuel and oxygen mix in the combustion chamber; the ignited fuel becomes a high-pressure gas expelled at very high velocity (Fig. 2.18). The gas and rocket push against each other and move in opposite directions: the rocket gains momentum equal to the momentum of the expelled gas but in the opposite direction (conservation of momentum). As the engines keep expelling gas, the rocket keeps gaining momentum and gets faster and faster.

No air needed: a rocket carries its own fuel as liquid or solid hydrogen and oxygen, so it works at great heights where there is little or no air. A typical rocket consumes about 10000 kg s⁻¹ of fuel and ejects burnt gases at over 4000 m s⁻¹.

Linked rockets: more than 80% of the launch mass is fuel. The rocket is made of several rockets linked together; when one has done its job it is discarded, and the others carry the craft further at ever greater speed.

Acceleration: if m is the mass of gas ejected per second with velocity v relative to the rocket, the change in momentum per second of the gas is mv, which equals the thrust on the rocket. So
a = mv/M
where M is the mass of the rocket. As fuel is burned and ejected, M decreases, so the acceleration increases.

book_ref.quote: Rockets move by expelling burning gas through engines at their rear.

blocks.prompt: 32 A rocket ejects 10000 kg of burnt gas per second at 4000 m s⁻¹ relative to it. Find the thrust and its acceleration (a = mv/M) when its mass is (i) 5.0 × 10⁶ kg (ii) 2.5 × 10⁶ kg. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Thrust = change in momentum of the gas per second = mv; divide by the rocket's mass for each case.

book_ref.quote: This equals the thrust produced by the engine on the body of the rocket.

steps: Thrust = mv = 10000 kg s⁻¹ × 4000 m s⁻¹ = 4.0 × 10⁷ N
blocks.final_answer: Thrust = 4.0 × 10⁷ N; a = 8.0 m s⁻² at 5.0 × 10⁶ kg and 16 m s⁻² at 2.5 × 10⁶ kg (the acceleration doubles as the mass halves)
